File:Blank Notebook Given to Charles Lin.description: This small notebook was made in Czechoslovakia around the mid 1920s and was sold by the Hampshire Book Shop of Northampton, Massachusetts. The book was given to Charles A. Lindbergh in 1927 by Estelle Carpenter, the director of music for the San Francisco public schools, on behalf of herself and the students of the San Francisco schools. Her business card and a handwritten note appear near the back of the blank book: "Miss Estelle Carpenter / Director of Music, of / San Francisco / Public School. / and all Pupils / of San Francisco / Cal." Lindbergh loaned the book to the Missouri Historical Society in 1927, and he gave it to the Society in 1933.

File:Bottle of water from the River Jord.description: Contained in the glass bottle on the left is water collected from the River Jordan at the site were Jesus Christ was believed to have been baptised by John the Baptist. The account is recorded in the New Testament of the Bible. Pilgrims visiting this holy area will often collect samples of the water – for its perceived medicinal and health-giving qualities as a souvenir of their pilgrimage. The bottle is shown here with a similar example (A6033). maker: Unknown maker Place made: Jordan Wellcome Images Keywords: baptism; bottle

File:Bottle of medicinal water, France,.api_title: File:Bottle of medicinal water, France, 1928 Wellcome L0057444.jpg
File:Bottle of medicinal water, France,.description: The bottle of medicinal water on the far left was collected from the hot spring of St Roch at the spa town of Bagnères de Bigorre in south-west France. Hot springs and mineral waters were popular in a number of ancient cultures – including Greek and Roman. Centuries later, a renewed interest in the healing and medicinal properties of these natural waters reached a peak in the Victorian period with hundreds of sites across Europe packed with visitors coming to ‘take the waters’ in the hope of a cure. The handwritten label gives the date, “17 March 1928”, the temperature of the spring, “47ºC” (117ºF), and indicates that it is to be used for the nerves. Once cooled the water was either drunk or applied to the body. St Roch, a pilgrim from Montpellier, France, during the 1300s, was said to cure plague and other infectious diseases. As a saint, he is one of several who was commonly invoked against the plague. The bottle is shown here with three others from the same region of France (A103805, A103806, A103807). maker: Unknown maker Place made: Bagnères de Bigorre, Hautes-Pyrénées, Midi-Pyrénées, France Wellcome Images Keywords: spa; medicinal water; bottle

File:Headset computer with phone as mous.description: A headset computer is a wearable personal computer that places a transparent near-eye OLED display in the user’s field of view, with adjustable brightness and transparency. The display module includes forward-facing cameras, an illumination light, and a microphone. The visor assembly can rotate upward over the head to move the screen out of view when not in use. The system uses a tethered pocket-PC for processing, battery power, wireless data, and I/O, connected by a USB-C cable routed under the user’s clothing, with audio delivered through a single-ear speaker. A smartphone can function as the primary pointing device by using its camera and flash for surface tracking and by interpreting taps and swipes on the touchscreen as mouse inputs, or could also be used as a trackpad. A future implementation could integrate a dedicated optical navigation sensor into the back of the phone to improve tracking resolution and responsiveness, using the small clearance naturally provided by many phone cases. The setup can be paired with compact portable keyboards that include protective covers with integrated batteries and can also be used with tablets such as iPads. The system would initially function primarily as a conventional personal computer, while augmented reality applications could be developed using the forward-facing cameras and onboard sensors.
